episodes.203067: Multiple supercells trekked across southeast Wyoming and the Nebraska panhandle the afternoon and evening of June 18th. Storms produced all form of severe weather including large hail, strong winds, funnel clouds, and urban flooding.
episodes.203068: Multiple supercells trekked across southeast Wyoming and the Nebraska panhandle the afternoon and evening of June 18th. Storms produced all form of severe weather including large hail, strong winds, funnel clouds, and urban flooding.
episodes.203098: An unstable atmosphere along with plenty of moisture led to the development of showers and thunderstorms. The thunderstorms were slow moving, and trained over the same areas in spots resulting in flash flooding. Rainfall amounts of one to locally four inches were observed in Northwest. Rainfall from the Sligo Creek watershed resulted in a rapid rise along the Anacostia River, while rainfall on the Rock Creek watershed resulted in a rapid rise along Rock Creek.
episodes.203103: Strong thunderstorms became severe as they moved from McCone County through Prairie County.
episodes.203107: An unstable atmosphere along with plenty of moisture led to the development of showers and thunderstorms. The thunderstorms were slow moving, and trained over the same areas in spots resulting in flash flooding. Localized rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed, with upwards of 5 inches in the most persistent thunderstorms.
episodes.203110: An unstable atmosphere along with plenty of moisture led to the development of showers and thunderstorms. The thunderstorms were slow moving, and trained over the same areas in spots resulting in flash flooding. Localized rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed, with upwards of 5 inches in the most persistent thunderstorms.
episodes.203121: An anomalously moist tropical airmass resided over Virginia bringing numerous rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Thunderstorms trained over portions of central Virginia bringing rainfall amounts of two to locally six inches. This resulted in instances of flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.203256: Several clusters of thunderstorms moved through Eastern NC through the evening. One storm became severe and produced damaging winds near Fairfield.
episodes.203355: A cold front sagged down through the Ohio Valley region, stalling out as a stationary front. Showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary in a very moist environment, producing heavy rainfall and flooding.
episodes.203409: Widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along and out ahead of a surface trough located in the Coastal Plain during the afternoon and evening of July Eighteenth. Once storms developed, they tracked southeastwards through the early evening before gradually dissipating after sunset. With ample instability in place, a few isolated storms became strong in nature bringing strong wind gusts to portions of the Albemarle and Pamlico Sounds.
episodes.203411: A surface trough was centered over the Coastal Plain during the afternoon and evening of July nineteenth. Showers and thunderstorms developed along and to the east of this surface trough with a few of these storms becoming strong in nature as they tracked south and east across Eastern North Carolina. The strongest storms impacted the waters along and north of Hatteras Island.
episodes.203511: A supercell developed north of a warm front during the early morning hours on Saturday (7/19).  The storm tracked from the Merrill area (Lincoln Co.) southeast towards Aniwa (Shawano Co.) producing damaging winds and hail up to golf ball size. 4 injuries were reported as a result of these storms.
episodes.203514: Thunderstorms tracked through east-central Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on Saturday (7/19).  The storms spun up a brief tornado in Manitowoc County as a thunderstorm interacted with the lake breeze boundary.
episodes.203775: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced localized damaging wind gusts over Albemarle County.
episodes.203828: Scattered thunderstorms produced localized flooding in parts of northwest Indiana during the afternoon of July 19th.
episodes.203934: A weak northern stream shortwave trough moving through the northwest CONUS resulted in the development of high based convection. Some of this convection resulted in strong to severe wind gusts. Additionally, a cutoff low placed off of the southwest CONUS helped advect moisture into southern Utah, leading to convection with periods of sufficiently heavy rain to result in flash flooding over some rain sensitive areas.
episodes.203975: A frontal boundary approaching from the north combined with a hot and humid air mass to produce isolated severe thunderstorms across northwest North Carolina. Damaging wind gusts from these storms blew down a few trees and power lines.
episodes.203976: A hot and humid air mass combined with orographical lift to produce a severe thunderstorm in Caswell County of northwest North Carolina. Damaging wind gusts from this storm blew down two trees.
episodes.204143: Clusters of thunderstorms developed during the morning hours just after sunrise across north Alabama. Strong and gusty winds produced sporadic wind damage, including trees being knocked down and a metal roof of a shed being torn off.
episodes.204235: In the afternoon of the 19th, a broken line of storms extended from extreme southwestern Nebraska into eastern Colorado across northwestern Kansas. This initial wave of storms produced hail up to one inch and 60 MPH winds. Additional storms formed in the evening and overnight hours from the earlier storms, and created winds up to 94 MPH, causing property damage.
episodes.204289: In the afternoon of the 19th, a broken line of storms extended from extreme southwestern Nebraska into eastern Colorado across northwestern Kansas. This initial wave of storms produced hail up to nickel sized and 62 MPH winds.
episodes.204353: Isolated thunderstorms forced by a weak low-level jet moved into west-central Illinois during the early morning hours of July 19th. One thunderstorm intensified as it passed over Pittsfield, causing a tree to fall onto a home. No injuries or deaths were reported.
episodes.204558: On July 17th, a west to east oriented cold front dropped southeast from the Midwest and stalled along the Ohio River. Multiple waves of convection along the front continued moving west to east across southern Indiana before the front lifted back north on July 20th. Isolated flooding issues were observed in multiple counties.
episodes.204559: On July 17th, a west to east oriented cold front dropped southeast from the Midwest and stalled along the Ohio River. Multiple waves of convection along the front continued moving west to east across central Kentucky before the front lifted back north on July 20th. Some isolated flooding issues and downed trees were observed in multiple counties.
episodes.204659: An upper-level disturbance moved across central North Carolina, triggering storms that produced damaging wind gusts and a few reports of flash flooding.
episodes.204704: Slow-moving thunderstorms dropped very heavy rainfall across southern Clay County from mid-morning through mid-afternoon of July 19th.  Rainfall amounts of 6-8 inches were common along and south of US-50, resulting in significant flash flooding from Xenia to Flora.  Further north, rainfall of 3-4 inches caused minor street flooding in parts of Decatur in Macon County.
episodes.204734: An Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved through the US 30 corridor resulting in flooding rain on its northern edge. The Northern Indiana NWS office recorded 0.72 of rain in just under 15 minutes. Rain totals of 3 to nearly 5 inches was common in La Porte, St. Joseph, Elkhart, De Kalb, and Noble Counties.
episodes.205048: Debris flow under saturated soils promoted resulted in a fallen tree on Road 139 at KM 18.2 in Sector Carmelita in Ponce. Rainfall accumulations are estimated at approximately 5 inches over the past few days, with an additional 1.30 inches recorded that day (July 18th).
episodes.205424: Scattered storms developed along an instability gradient across western Minnesota during the late afternoon into early evening. The environment was lacking instability overall, so while several storms were strong only one produced severe weather.||Several reports of large hail were recorded with the storm that tracked through southeastern Stearns county. The largest hail size was 2 inches in diameter (lime-sized).
episodes.205425: On the afternoon of July 19, 2025, a weak surface boundary lingered over northeast Nebraska. An approaching disturbance triggered storms along this boundary, which intensified rapidly. One of these storms was a supercell that split, with a left-moving supercell heading into Knox County and a right-moving supercell moving into Antelope County. While the right-moving storm quickly weakened, the left-moving storm persisted, producing hail up to 1 inch in diameter at 3:28 PM CST, as reported by a trained spotter. The storm gradually weakened as it moved to the northeast.
episodes.205451: A decaying line of thunderstorms moved into Benton County on the morning of July 19th. This produced heavy rain with trained spotters reports ranging from 1.5 to 3.5 inches of rain. This rain falling on already saturated ground led to flash flooding in Vinton.
episodes.205484: A decaying line of thunderstorms moved into Muscatine on the morning of July 19th. This produced heavy rain with trained spotters reports ranging from 3 to 4 inches of rain. This rain falling on already saturated ground led to flash flooding in Macomb.
episodes.205526: Isolated thunderstorms over the Cumberland plateau produced some locally heavy rains and flash flooding in far northwest Sequatchie county.
episodes.205588: A surface boundary was positioned west to east across the Quad State during the early afternoon with convective activity increasing with daytime heating. Scattered convection primarily occurred south of the boundary mid to late afternoon. MLCAPE reached 2000J/kg but effective bulk shear was very limited. Precipitable water values over 2 allowed for torrential rainfall rates. Training storm occurrence was limited, leaving flash flooding south of Harrisburg as the one flood report out of Southern Illinois.
episodes.205589: A surface boundary was positioned west to east across the Quad State during the early afternoon with convective activity increasing with daytime heating. Scattered convection primarily occurred south of the boundary mid to late afternoon. MLCAPE reached 2000-3000J/kg but effective bulk shear was very limited. Precipitable water values over 2 allowed for torrential rainfall rates. Training storm activity occurred near sunset in the Evansville/Newburgh area as isolated storms developed over the area followed by a more organized storm line. Significant flash flooding developed on the southeast side of Evanvsille and western parts of Newburgh with several streets covered by more than a foot of water. Several water rescues took place into the early evening.
episodes.205590: A surface boundary was positioned west to east across the Quad State during the early afternoon with convective activity increasing with daytime heating. Scattered convection primarily occurred south of the boundary mid to late afternoon. MLCAPE reached 2000-3000J/kg but effective bulk shear was very limited. Precipitable water values over 2 allowed for torrential rainfall rates. Training storm activity was limited in Western Kentucky, though flash flooding was observed in Paducah and areal flooding observed near Henderson and Owensboro. A retired NWS meteorologist measured 2.78 in 50 minutes in Reidland. While severe thunderstorm activity was very limited, Western Kentucky did have wind damage in Paducah and a 52mph gust was measured at the Madisonville AWOS.
episodes.205592: As high pressure slowly crept northward towards the Quad State region, ridging remained over the middle Mississippi River Valley. A slow-moving MCS moved through the northeastern half of the Quad State midday to near sunset. CAPE rose to 1000-2000J/kg in northern portions of Southern Illinois with effective bulk shear around 30kts. Extremely high moisture content with precipitable water values of 2.25in resulted in torrential rainfall rates along and near the I-64 corridor. Several areas reported flash flooding, especially northern Wayne County which had radar estimated totals of up to half a foot in northwestern portions of the county and sandbags deployed in Cisne. Flash flooding was also reported in Hamilton, Franklin, and Williamson counties. Albion reported 3.12in of rainfall within four hours.
episodes.205594: As high pressure slowly crept northward towards the Quad State region, ridging remained over the middle Mississippi River Valley. A slow-moving MCS moved through the northeastern half of the Quad State midday to near sunset. CAPE rose to 1000-2000J/kg in Southwest Indiana with effective bulk shear around 30kts. Extremely high moisture content with precipitable water values of 2.25in resulted in torrential rainfall rates in Southwest Indiana. Each of the six counties in Southwest Indiana reported flash flooding. In Gibson County, street flooding occurred in Francisco mid-late morning, with a gage reporting 4.25in of rain 3 miles NW of Francisco. Pike County had some of the longest lasting flooding as a widespread area saw 2-3.5 during the morning hours. Spencer County received 2.5-4 of rain in and around Rockport, with flooding there lingering towards sunset. More isolated flooding issues occurred in Posey, Vanderburgh, and Warrick Counties with Evansville area flooding generally on the north and east sides of the airport.
episodes.205595: As high pressure slowly crept northward towards the Quad State region, ridging remained over the middle Mississippi River Valley. A slow-moving MCS moved through the northeastern half of the Quad State midday to near sunset. CAPE rose to 2000-3000J/kg but shear remained limited in Western Kentucky. Extremely high moisture content with precipitable water values of 2.2in resulted in torrential rainfall rate potential but intensity decreased late afternoon as the storm line dropped into Western Kentucky. Flooding was reported in Union County, while a tree was felled by thunderstorm winds in Hopkins County.
episodes.205596: Isolated thunderstorms developed along a surface boundary from Brown County, west southwest into Arthur County during the early evening hours of July 18th. Storms became severe over central Brown County, leading to three brief tornadoes. Later in the evening, quarter sized hail was reported northwest of Burwell in Garfield County.
episodes.205598: Thunderstorms developed along a stationary front, situated across the Nebraska Sandhills during the mid afternoon hours of July 19th. Storms quickly became severe over McPherson, Logan and northern Lincoln Counties around 3 PM CDT. Over the next couple of hours, activity expanded east and west of the initial storms becoming severe. Later in the early evening hours, additional activity developed over northern Brown County, quickly becoming severe. Hail up to 4 inches in diameter was reported in far northern Lincoln and southern Logan Counties. Hail up to 3 inches in diameter was reported in western McPherson Count and in Eustis in Frontier County. Thunderstorm wind damage was also reported in northern Brown County, impacting the Ainsworth area.
episodes.205760: A stationary front was draped north of the region with several embedded disturbances aloft moving across the area, resulting in heavy rainfall and flash flooding.
episodes.205761: A stationary front was draped north of the region with several embedded disturbances aloft moving across the area, resulting in widespread strong winds and some isolated severe hail.
episodes.205804: A stationary front was draped north of the region with several embedded disturbances aloft moving across the area, resulting in widespread strong winds to the local waters.
episodes.205834: A shortwave crossed central Wyoming and brought localized severe weather. A 62 mph wind gust was reported along Interstate 25 near Midwest in northern Natrona County. A Cocorahs member reported penny size hail southwest of Powell. In the evening, a 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Pistol Draw RAWS site.
episodes.205915: A high based shower collapsed near the Riverton airport produced a 58 mph wind gust.
episodes.205988: An EF1 tornado impacted a home and adjacent homestead off of Grey Rd in far western Crook county. The tornado produced EF0 damage to several outbuildings south of the main single family residence. EF0 consisted of pushing and destroying a small shed outbuilding and pushing a storage silo off its pad and rotating it 45 degrees to the SW from its origin. The tornado tracked NE and continued to produce EF0 damage near the main home. Several trees near the home were snapped and the home loss some roofing material. The tornado continued to the NE before shifting to the ENE where it intensified to EF1. The tornado damaged a large outbuilding, ripping two concrete foots out of the ground and pushing the entire concrete brace from the foundation some 10 yards to the ENE. The entire structure had slid off the foundation with the structures walls all collapsed. The tornado then entered open field with no damage indicators available. A large debris field of tree branches and building material was thrown to the E, NE and N of the tornado track.
episodes.206066: Outflow from a modest complex of thunderstorms moved across Alabama northeast into Georgia. The leading edge was able to tap into increased CAPE near the ATL metro and produced a small corridor of 60 mph winds just north of the city.
episodes.206069: A stationary front was anchored north of the area in Pennsylvania. Deep moisture was in place to the south of the front with precipitable water values near two inches. Strong surface heating resulted in robust instability with wind shear around 25 knots, allowing for deep, slow moving, convection capable of heavy rainfall and flash flooding during the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.206074: A stationary front was anchored north of the area in Pennsylvania. Deep moisture was in place to the south of the front with precipitable water values near two inches. Strong surface heating resulted in robust instability with wind shear around 25 knots, allowing for deep, slow moving, convection capable of heavy rainfall and flash flooding during the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.206075: A stationary front was anchored north of the area in Pennsylvania. Deep moisture was in place to the south of the front with precipitable water values near two inches. Strong surface heating resulted in robust instability with wind shear around 25 knots, allowing for deep convection with strong downdraft winds during the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.206084: A stationary front was anchored north of the area in Pennsylvania. Deep moisture was in place to the south of the front with precipitable water values near two inches. Strong surface heating resulted in robust instability with wind shear around 25 knots, allowing for deep convection with strong downdraft winds during the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.206099: Weak low pressure moving up from the south brought a finger of monsoon moisture to the Mojave Desert, fueling scattered thunderstorms. One storm produced heavy rain which led to water rescues in concrete flood channels, and one produced high winds.
episodes.206159: A shortwave passed across the area the previous evening with a trailing boundary that dove south across the area through the early morning hours of July 19th. Strong theta e advection in the warm sector ahead of the boundary created an unstable environment with 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE with 30-40 kts of 0-6 km shear. Storms developed along this boundary across northern Iowa and quickly pushed south through sunrise, fueled by the low level jet. Wind was the primary hazard with the line of storms and in most cases it remained sub severe, however acceleration in central Iowa near sunrise resulted in gusts of 60 to 70 mph. At the same time a cell merger occurred along the leading edge of storms. This merger resulted in a brief enhancement with tornadogenesis. This tornado developed in Boone county and tracked through cropland, crossing into Story county before dissipating just before reaching the community of Gilbert. Despite the tornado dissipating, straight line winds remained strong and resulted in some damage within Gilbert.
episodes.206169: A cluster of thunderstorms developed north of U.S. Highway 14 near the South Dakota-Minnesota border during the evening of July 18. These thunderstorms drifted south and east along a slow-moving surface boundary and began to train/back-build across the Marshall, MN area. Four to eight inches of rain fell within 2 to 3 hours, resulting in significant flash flooding across the city, especially for areas south and east of downtown.
episodes.206232: A slow moving line of storms produced heavy rainfall across portions of southern Minnesota, especially over Blue Earth County. Widespread rain persisted for about 1.5 to 2.5 hours with rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour at times. The rain began just before midnight on the 18th and continued into the 19th.
episodes.206384: A single thunderstorm passed over rural Sheridan County, which downed some power lines and caused tree damage.
episodes.206385: Strong thunderstorms occurred across far southeast Montana, producing gusts up to 65 mph and hail up to golf ball size.

Multiple rounds of thunderstorms pass across portions of Carroll County and the City of Galax during the afternoon of the 19th, with rainfall rates occasionally spiking to nearly 6 inches per hour. Among the reports of flooding that occurred in this area, a small tributary of Chestnut Creek over flowed its banks and flooded several inches deep across a portion of Cliffview Road. Dixon Branch was also observed overflowing its banks across part of Fries Road.  A portion of Hebron Road was flooded and became impassible for a short period of time by flooding of Little Cranberry Creek, and Mill Creek overflowed its banks across Glade Street.  No damage was reported to the roads, which were open to traffic after the water receded.

Flash flooding occurred at Heritage Hills Point West Trailer Park. Water was about 15in deep, and several trailers were surrounded by water. Nearby, part of the intersection of Lincoln Ave and Lenn Rd was covered.
Flooding was reported on Interstate 94 between State Road 249 and Route 20.

A tornado touched down north of Branch at 4:21 PM CDT.  The tornado tracked southeast and snapped and uprooted some trees and produced siding and roofing damage near the start of the tornado, tracking over farm fields with damage evident on satellite data before dissipating just northeast of Branch at 4:25 PM CDT. Total path length is estimated to be 1.58 miles long, with a width of 60 yards.  Peak wind estimated to be around 77 mph.
Several trees fell down across the road, blocking all lanes.

Severe thunderstorms producing several wet microbursts, led to violent winds in Ainsworth. Wind gusts, estimated at around 100 MPH, uprooted several mature trees in and around Ainsworth. Other mature trees were snapped above ground level. Numerous reports of power lines down, one of which, led to fire at a residence on the north side of Ainsworth.  One house sustained significant damage as a mature tree impacted the roof of this residence.

The river gauge upstream along Rock Creek rose about 6 feet within an hour. The water was estimated to have flowed through the rest of Rock Creek into the Potomac River, causing rapid rises along the way.

The river gauge upstream along Sligo Creek rose about 6 feet within an hour. Montgomery County Emergency Management indicated about 10 foot rises in the same area with their gauges. This water drains into the Anacostia River. The water was estimated to have flowed through the rest of the Anacostia into the Potomac River, causing rapid rises along the way.
